questions.stem: The Middle Kingdom began when Egypt was reunified by Mentuhotep II, who came from:
options: Herakleopolis, in Middle Egypt
Avaris, in the eastern Delta
Thebes, in Upper Egypt
Memphis, at the head of the Delta
questions.explanation: Mentuhotep II of the Theban Eleventh Dynasty defeated the rival kings of Herakleopolis and reunited the country. This made Thebes, a provincial town in the Old Kingdom, a centre of power.

questions.stem: Mentuhotep II changed his Horus name during his reign, finally taking one meaning ‘he who unites the Two Lands’. This was mainly intended to:
options: show that he had given up any claim to rule over Lower Egypt
honour the Herakleopolitan kings he had defeated in the civil war
mark his retirement from the throne in favour of his eldest son
announce his reunification of Egypt as the basis of his authority
questions.explanation: Royal names were statements of policy. Taking a name that celebrated the union of the Two Lands presented the end of the civil wars as his great achievement and linked him to the ideal of Old Kingdom unity.

questions.stem: Mentuhotep II addressed a weakness that had helped bring down the Old Kingdom. He did this by:
options: moving the capital to Avaris so the king could watch over the Delta nomes
handing the collection of taxes to the temples of the god Re at Heliopolis
reducing the independence of the nomarchs and relying on royal court officials
making the office of nomarch hereditary so that the local ruling families would stay loyal
questions.explanation: The Old Kingdom had weakened as hereditary nomarchs kept resources for themselves. Mentuhotep II subordinated provincial governors to senior officials of his own court, such as governors of Upper and Lower Egypt, and centralised government again.

questions.stem: Statues and reliefs show Mentuhotep II with the attributes of gods, and his titles stress his divine nature. Historians interpret this ‘self-deification’ mainly as:
options: evidence that Egyptians had never seen their kings as divine before
a sign that the priests of Amun now controlled the whole of the king's government
a copy of the Hyksos practice of worshipping their kings as gods
a way to restore royal authority after a long period of divided rule
questions.explanation: After the First Intermediate Period, the king needed to re-establish his sacred status above the nomarchs and rival dynasties. Old Kingdom kings had already been seen as divine; Mentuhotep II was reasserting and emphasising that idea. The Hyksos came centuries later.

questions.stem: Which statement best describes the balance of continuity and change in Mentuhotep II's reign?
options: He revived Old Kingdom ideals of kingship but built a new kind of mortuary temple
He copied the Old Kingdom in every way, including building a pyramid at Giza for his tomb
He broke completely with the Old Kingdom and abandoned the idea of a divine king
He kept Egypt divided into two kingdoms but ruled both from the city of Memphis
questions.explanation: Mentuhotep II looked back to the united, divine kingship of the Old Kingdom, but instead of a pyramid he built a terraced temple at Deir el-Bahri. This mix of continuity and change is central to this period.

questions.stem: Mentuhotep II built his mortuary temple at Deir el-Bahri, which is:
options: on the west bank of the Nile opposite Thebes
on the east bank of the Nile, beside the old capital of Memphis
on the coast of the Delta near the sea
on an island at the First Cataract
questions.explanation: Deir el-Bahri is a bay in the cliffs on the west bank at Thebes, near what would become the Valley of the Kings. The west, where the sun set, was associated with the dead.

questions.stem: Mentuhotep II's mortuary temple differed from Old Kingdom royal tombs because it was:
options: a small chapel with no connection to the king's burial
a terraced temple with colonnades set against the cliffs
a true pyramid built of limestone blocks out in the open desert
a mastaba of mud brick in the cemetery of Saqqara
questions.explanation: Instead of a pyramid, Mentuhotep II built a terraced temple with pillared halls, set into the cliffs, with his burial cut into the rock behind it. Later kings such as Hatshepsut built beside it and echoed its design.

questions.stem: In 1900 Howard Carter's horse stumbled into a hole at Deir el-Bahri, leading to the discovery of the Bab el-Hosan. There he found:
options: the intact tomb of Tutankhamun with its gold coffins
the sarcophagus of a Hyksos king buried along with his chariot
a copy of the Story of Sinuhe written on papyrus
a seated statue of Mentuhotep II wearing the red crown
questions.explanation: The Bab el-Hosan contained a large seated statue of Mentuhotep II wearing the red crown, painted with a black-skinned body, a colour linked to Osiris and rebirth. Carter found Tutankhamun's tomb in the Valley of the Kings in 1922.

questions.stem: Herbert Winlock found the bodies of about sixty soldiers, many with wounds from arrows and clubs, in a tomb near Mentuhotep II's temple. A historian could best use this as evidence that:
options: Egyptian armies of the period already fought with horse chariots and bronze armour
Mentuhotep II himself was killed in battle and buried among his soldiers
reunification involved real warfare, and the king honoured soldiers who died for him
the soldiers were executed for disloyalty and buried away from the king's temple
questions.explanation: The wounds show violent deaths in battle, and burial close to the royal temple suggests honour. This supports the view that reunification came through war. Chariots arrived only with the Hyksos period, and Mentuhotep II was buried in his own tomb.

questions.stem: Winlock's excavations near Deir el-Bahri also uncovered the wooden models from the tomb of the official Meketre. They are valuable because they show:
options: the battles in which Mentuhotep II defeated the kings of Herakleopolis
the Hyksos capital at Avaris as it looked before its fall
daily activities such as counting cattle, baking and sailing
the plans the architects used to design the royal temple
questions.explanation: The Meketre models show granaries, workshops, boats, a cattle count and a garden, giving a three-dimensional view of the estate and economy of a high official. Like tomb scenes, they show an ideal provision for the afterlife.

questions.stem: Amenemhat I, first king of the Twelfth Dynasty, moved the royal capital from Thebes to:
options: Itjtawy, near Lisht
Avaris, in the Delta
Abydos, in the south
Alexandria, on the coast
questions.explanation: Amenemhat I founded Itjtawy near Lisht, close to the junction of Upper and Lower Egypt, a better place to govern the whole country. Its name means roughly ‘Amenemhat seizes the Two Lands’.

questions.stem: The Twelfth Dynasty introduced co-regency, in which:
options: the vizier ruled Egypt while the king was a child
the king and the high priest of Amun shared power
the ruling king made his heir a joint king before he died
two unrelated royal families took turns to hold the throne of Egypt
questions.explanation: By making his son a co-ruler during his lifetime, a king secured a smooth succession and reduced the risk of rivals seizing the throne. This mattered to a new dynasty, such as Amenemhat I's, whose founder was not of royal birth.

questions.stem: The Sed festival was a royal ritual that:
options: marked the annual start of the Nile flood at the First Cataract near Aswan
celebrated the burial of a king and the crowning of his successor
honoured the Hyksos kings who ruled Lower Egypt from Avaris
renewed the king's strength and right to rule, often after 30 years
questions.explanation: The Sed festival, or jubilee, renewed the king's physical and divine power, traditionally first celebrated in his thirtieth year. Kings recorded it in temples and art as proof of a long, strong reign.

questions.stem: The Prophecy of Neferti is set at the court of the Old Kingdom king Sneferu. A sage foretells a time of chaos, ended by a king called Ameny from the south. The text was most likely written to:
options: warn Middle Kingdom kings not to trust officials from the south
criticise Amenemhat I for causing chaos when he seized the throne
legitimise Amenemhat I by presenting his rule as foretold and destined
record a real prophecy spoken during Sneferu's reign and passed down unchanged
questions.explanation: ‘Ameny’ is a short form of Amenemhat. Setting the prophecy far in the past made his rise seem destined and presented him as the saviour who restored order. This is classic Middle Kingdom royal propaganda.

questions.stem: In the Instructions of King Amenemhat, the dead king speaks to his son and warns him to:
options: trust no one, because those close to him turned against him
rely on the nomarchs, because they had always been loyal to his family
give up the throne and live a quiet life outside the court
build a pyramid at Giza like those of the Fourth Dynasty
questions.explanation: The text describes an attack on Amenemhat I by members of his own household and advises Senwosret I to trust no brother and know no friend. It presents the new king as the rightful heir and justifies firm rule.

questions.stem: In the Story of Sinuhe, an official flees Egypt after Amenemhat I's death, prospers in the Levant, but longs to return. In old age Senwosret I welcomes him home and grants him a tomb. Which message does the story most clearly promote?
options: Foreign lands such as the Levant were better places to live than Egypt itself
Kings of the Twelfth Dynasty had no interest in what happened to their officials
Loyalty to the king, and the belief that a good life must end with burial in Egypt
Disloyalty to the king is always rewarded with wealth and honour in foreign lands
questions.explanation: The story celebrates the king's mercy and the value of being buried in Egypt with proper rites. It shows Senwosret I as generous and Egypt as superior. Sinuhe's success abroad is not enough; he longs to come home.

questions.stem: The Lay of the Harper, a song from a tomb, urges listeners to enjoy life because no one returns from death. Historians find it significant because it:
options: describes the rituals of mummification in exact and careful step-by-step detail
records the names and reigns of every king of the Twelfth Dynasty
proves that Egyptians stopped building tombs in the Middle Kingdom
expresses doubt about the afterlife that contrasts with official beliefs
questions.explanation: The song's advice to ‘follow your heart’ and its doubt about tombs and the afterlife show a range of attitudes in Egyptian thought, not only the confident beliefs in official religious texts. It does not record king lists or mummification.

questions.stem: A student argues that Middle Kingdom literature such as the Story of Sinuhe and the Prophecy of Neferti is unreliable and of no use to historians. Which response is best?
options: It is reliable because it was written by eyewitnesses to each of the events it describes
It is of no use, because literary works cannot tell us anything about the past
It is useful only for showing the everyday lives of Egyptian farmers and labourers
It is useful for showing the values and image of kingship the court wished to spread
questions.explanation: Even when the events are invented or shaped, the literature reveals what the royal court valued: loyalty, order, a just king and the superiority of Egypt. Its usefulness depends on the question asked of it.

questions.stem: Middle Kingdom Egypt imported cedar wood, valuable for ships and coffins, mainly from:
options: Crete, in the Aegean Sea
Byblos, on the Levantine coast
Punt, on the Red Sea coast
Kerma, the capital of the kingdom of Kush
questions.explanation: Cedar came from the mountains of Lebanon through the port of Byblos, a long-standing trade partner. Punt supplied incense and exotic goods, and Nubia gold and ivory.

questions.stem: Pottery made on Crete has been found at Middle Kingdom sites in Egypt such as Lahun. This is evidence that:
options: Egypt was conquered by a fleet from the island of Crete
Egypt had contact and trade with the Aegean world
Cretan settlers ruled the Faiyum in the Middle Kingdom
Egyptian potters copied Cretan pots for their own tombs
questions.explanation: Minoan pottery in Egypt, along with finds such as the Tod treasure, shows Egypt drawn into wider Mediterranean exchange in the Middle Kingdom. Imported goods alone do not show conquest or foreign rule.

questions.stem: A painting in the tomb of the nomarch Khnumhotep II at Beni Hasan shows a group of Asiatics, led by a man named Abisha, arriving in Egypt with goods. It is best used as evidence of:
options: contact and trade between Egypt and peoples of the Levant
the Hyksos conquest of Lower Egypt and the fall of Itjtawy
the capture of Asiatic prisoners in a Nubian campaign
the expulsion of all foreigners from Egypt by Senwosret II
questions.explanation: The scene shows people from western Asia bringing eye paint and other goods, recorded as a peaceful visit. It is evidence of contact with western Asia and of people moving into Egypt, part of the background to the later Hyksos settlement in the Delta.

questions.stem: Middle Kingdom kings built a chain of large mud-brick fortresses in Nubia, such as Buhen and Semna, at the:
options: Second Cataract
Nile Delta
Red Sea coast
Sinai Peninsula
questions.explanation: The fortresses at and around the Second Cataract controlled the river, trade in gold and other goods, and the movement of Nubians. They marked Egypt's southern frontier.

questions.stem: Egypt's main reason for conquering and controlling Lower Nubia in the Middle Kingdom was to:
options: secure gold and trade goods and guard the frontier against Kush
gain new land to grow wheat because Egypt's own fields had failed
find cedar trees to build ships for the Mediterranean trade
spread the worship of Osiris to the people of the Levant
questions.explanation: Nubia had gold mines and was the route for ivory, ebony and other goods from Africa, while the kingdom of Kush based at Kerma was a growing rival. Fortresses protected both trade and the frontier. Cedar came from Lebanon.

questions.stem: Senwosret III's boundary stele at Semna describes Nubians as cowards who flee when attacked, and says that any son of his who keeps this boundary is truly his son. The stele is best interpreted as:
options: proof that the Nubians were never a serious threat to Middle Kingdom Egypt
a peace treaty that returned the land of Lower Nubia to its Nubian rulers
royal propaganda that justified conquest and urged heirs to defend the frontier
a neutral description of Nubian society written by a visiting Nubian scholar
questions.explanation: The stele presents the king's view, belittling the enemy to show royal strength, and charges future kings with holding the border. The heavy fortification of the region suggests the Nubians were taken seriously, despite the stele's scorn.

questions.stem: The god Amun, who became increasingly important from the Middle Kingdom, was originally a local god of:
options: Thebes
Memphis
Heliopolis
Abydos
questions.explanation: Amun rose to prominence because the Theban dynasties who reunited Egypt promoted their local god. Senwosret I's White Chapel at Karnak is an early royal monument to him. Heliopolis was the centre of Re's cult.

questions.stem: During the Middle Kingdom, many ordinary Egyptians set up stelae and offerings at Abydos because:
options: it was the only place where the Nile flood reached the desert edge
it was the site of the Hyksos capital, which they wished to honour
it was the cult centre of Osiris, where they hoped to share in his rebirth
it was the new capital city, where the king held his court each year at the flood
questions.explanation: Abydos was believed to hold the burial place of Osiris, and its annual festival drew people who wanted to be linked with his resurrection. This reflects wider access to the afterlife in the Middle Kingdom.

questions.stem: In the Middle Kingdom, spells once reserved for the king were painted inside the coffins of officials and nobles. These spells are known as the:
options: Coffin Texts
Pyramid Texts
Book of the Dead
Amarna Letters
questions.explanation: The Coffin Texts adapted royal Pyramid Texts for non-royal elites, showing wider access to the afterlife. The Book of the Dead is the New Kingdom development, and the Amarna Letters are diplomatic correspondence.

questions.stem: Twelfth Dynasty kings such as Senwosret II and Amenemhat III built pyramids, but these differed from Old Kingdom pyramids because they:
options: were much larger than the Great Pyramid and took a century to complete
had mud-brick cores faced with stone and complex passages to deter robbers
were built of solid granite blocks from top to bottom and had no passages
were cut into the cliffs at Deir el-Bahri rather than built in the desert
questions.explanation: Middle Kingdom pyramids used cheaper mud-brick cores with a limestone casing, and their builders designed hidden entrances and maze-like passages against tomb robbers. When the casing was removed, many crumbled.

questions.stem: Statues of Senwosret III show a lined, careworn face, unlike the calm, youthful faces of Old Kingdom kings. Which interpretation is most defensible?
options: It shows that Egyptians had stopped believing their kings were divine
It may present the king as burdened by the duties of protecting Egypt
It proves the king was ill and unable to rule for most of his reign
It shows that sculptors were no longer controlled by the royal court
questions.explanation: Historians debate whether the faces are realistic portraits or a deliberate image of a watchful, responsible ruler. Royal statues remained official works, so a careworn face still served the king's image. They cannot prove illness.

questions.stem: Which project is most associated with Amenemhat III?
options: Moving the capital of Egypt from Itjtawy back to Memphis
Land reclamation and irrigation works in the Faiyum
Building the Step Pyramid at Saqqara for his father
Expelling the Hyksos from Avaris and the eastern Delta
questions.explanation: Twelfth Dynasty kings, especially Senwosret II and Amenemhat III, developed the Faiyum, increasing farmland. Amenemhat III's pyramid complex at Hawara, near the Faiyum, was later described by Greek writers as the ‘Labyrinth’.

questions.stem: The rich tombs of nomarch families at sites such as Beni Hasan largely stop appearing around the reign of Senwosret III. Many historians use this to argue that:
options: Senwosret III gave the nomarchs more land in return for military service
Senwosret III was overthrown by the nomarchs of Middle Egypt
Senwosret III moved his court to Beni Hasan to be near his officials
Senwosret III reduced the power of the nomarchs and strengthened the crown
questions.explanation: The rich tombs of nomarch families largely stop appearing around Senwosret III's reign, which many historians read as evidence that he curbed provincial power. The exact reasons are debated, but the pattern fits greater central control.

questions.stem: In the late Middle Kingdom, Egypt was ruled by many short-reigned kings. The main consequence was that:
options: royal authority weakened as power slipped to officials and regional rulers
the king gained complete control over every one of the nomes for the first time
Egypt conquered the Levant and made Byblos its new capital city
the nomarchs lost all their land to the temples of the god Amun
questions.explanation: Rapid turnover of kings in the Thirteenth Dynasty weakened the throne, and power moved towards officials and regional rulers. Central authority declined, opening the way to the Second Intermediate Period.

questions.stem: The name ‘Hyksos’ comes from an Egyptian phrase meaning:
options: ‘shepherds of the desert’
‘sons of the god Seth’
‘people of the chariot’
‘rulers of foreign lands’
questions.explanation: Hyksos derives from heqau khasut, ‘rulers of foreign lands’. The later translation ‘shepherd kings’, found in the writer Josephus, is a mistake.

questions.stem: The Hyksos ruled Lower Egypt as the Fifteenth Dynasty from their capital at:
options: Thebes
Itjtawy
Memphis
Avaris
questions.explanation: Avaris, at modern Tell el-Dab'a in the eastern Delta, was the Hyksos capital. Thebes was the base of the Seventeenth Dynasty, which ruled Upper Egypt at the same time.

questions.stem: Excavations at Tell el-Dab'a, led by Manfred Bietak, found Levantine-style houses, pottery and burials built up over many generations. This evidence best supports the view that the Hyksos:
options: were western Asian settlers who grew powerful over time before taking control
were a sudden invading army that arrived from Mesopotamia in a single year
were Nubians from Kerma who had moved north along the Nile in search of land
were Egyptians from Thebes who adopted foreign customs to win over the Delta
questions.explanation: The gradual build-up of Levantine culture at Avaris suggests migration and settlement before the Hyksos took power, rather than the sudden invasion described in later accounts. This is now the view most historians hold.

questions.stem: The later Egyptian writer Manetho, as quoted by Josephus, described the Hyksos as invaders who burned cities and destroyed temples. Historians treat this account with caution mainly because:
options: it agrees in every detail with the archaeological evidence from Tell el-Dab'a
it was written over a thousand years later and reflects hostile Egyptian tradition
it was written by a Hyksos king who wished to make his people seem stronger
it was carved on the walls of Avaris during the reign of the Hyksos king Apepi
questions.explanation: Manetho wrote in the third century BCE, and his work survives only in later quotations. His account echoes the Theban view of the Hyksos as destructive foreigners, which the archaeology of gradual settlement does not support.

questions.stem: Which statement about the Hyksos kings is supported by the evidence?
options: They used Egyptian royal titles and hieroglyphs and worshipped the god Seth
They banned Egyptian writing and forced everyone to speak their own language
They destroyed every Egyptian temple and built Mesopotamian ziggurats instead
They refused to trade with Egypt's neighbours and closed the ports of the Delta
questions.explanation: Hyksos rulers adopted Egyptian kingship, titles and script, and honoured Seth, a god they linked with a storm god of their homeland. The Rhind Mathematical Papyrus was copied in the reign of the Hyksos king Apepi.

questions.stem: Which military innovation is most associated with the Hyksos period in Egypt?
options: The trireme warship and the bronze ram
The siege tower and the battering ram
The horse-drawn chariot and the composite bow
The war elephant and the long iron-tipped spear
questions.explanation: The horse and chariot and the powerful composite bow came into Egypt during the Hyksos period. The Egyptians used them to defeat the Hyksos and later to build a New Kingdom empire.

questions.stem: Historians argue that the Hyksos period changed Egypt's attitude to the outside world. Which consequence best supports this?
options: New Kingdom rulers built buffer territories in the Levant to stop foreign rule recurring
Egypt closed its borders and stopped all contact with the Levant after the Hyksos left
Egypt returned to being ruled by nomarchs, each with an army of foreign soldiers
Egyptian kings gave up war and relied only on trade to protect their borders
questions.explanation: Having experienced foreign rule, New Kingdom kings pushed into the Levant and Nubia, using the chariot warfare learned in this period. Egypt's earlier relative isolation gave way to empire.

questions.stem: The Tale of Apepi and Seqenenre describes the Hyksos king complaining that the noise of hippopotamuses at Thebes was keeping him awake. Historians read this as:
options: a joke told at Seqenenre's funeral to honour the Hyksos king
a provocation that the Theban story uses to explain the start of war
an accurate record of a peace treaty signed by Apepi and Seqenenre
evidence that the Hyksos kings lived in Thebes beside the Nile
questions.explanation: Avaris is hundreds of kilometres from Thebes, so the complaint is an absurd insult. The tale presents the Hyksos king as an arrogant aggressor and Seqenenre as provoked into conflict.

questions.stem: The mummy of the Theban king Seqenenre Tao has severe head wounds. These are usually taken as evidence that he:
options: died violently, most likely in conflict with the Hyksos
died of old age after a long and peaceful reign
was killed by a hippopotamus during a royal hunt on the Nile
was murdered by his own son to seize the throne
questions.explanation: The wounds, some consistent with axes of Asiatic style, suggest a violent death in the war against the Hyksos. Exactly how he died is debated, but the injuries rule out a peaceful end.

questions.stem: The Theban king Kamose recorded on stelae at Karnak that he intercepted a messenger from the Hyksos king Apepi to the ruler of Kush. Why was this message significant?
options: Apepi was inviting Kamose to a festival of Seth at the Hyksos capital
Apepi was seeking an alliance with Kush to attack Thebes from both sides
Apepi was offering to hand over Avaris to Kamose in exchange for gold
Apepi was asking Kush to send troops to defend Thebes against Nubia
questions.explanation: The intercepted letter proposed that Kush and the Hyksos divide Egypt, which would have trapped Thebes between enemies in the north and south. Kamose used the episode to justify his campaigns.

questions.stem: The tomb autobiography of Ahmose, son of Ebana, at Elkab is a key source for the defeat of the Hyksos because:
options: it is a Hyksos king's own account of why he surrendered Avaris
it is a royal decree listing every Hyksos king and his reign
it is a letter from Kush describing the Theban army's defeat
it is a soldier's own account of fighting at Avaris and Sharuhen
questions.explanation: Ahmose son of Ebana describes serving under King Ahmose at the siege of Avaris and the later siege of Sharuhen in southern Canaan, and being rewarded with the ‘gold of valour’. As a soldier's account it gives a perspective from below the king, though still celebrating Theban victory.

questions.stem: Why did Theban kings and later New Kingdom texts vilify the Hyksos?
options: To persuade the Hyksos to return and rule Egypt jointly with Thebes
To show that the Hyksos had greatly improved Egyptian religion and art
To record the Hyksos period accurately for future historians to study
To present Theban rule as the liberation of Egypt from foreign usurpers
questions.explanation: Portraying the Hyksos as foreign, impious oppressors made the Theban kings into national saviours and justified their power. Hatshepsut later claimed the Hyksos had ruled ‘without Re’. Such texts are propaganda, not neutral history.
